title: The work list
dek: What is being done here, as opposed to what is known.
lead: Every other page in this atlas answers what it holds. This one answers what is being done to it, including the parts that are stuck and the parts that were wrong. An item marked **struck** was founded on a mistake and is kept rather than deleted, because a work list that only records successes is a advertisement.
close: Nothing here is a research finding. Those belong on the map, the country pages and the surname pages. This is the state of the work.

rows.what: Walk every FamilySearch collection's waypoint tree
rows.note: **Running now.** 3,504 collections; the tree descends to the individual book. 707,471 volumes so far against 4,903 when the day started. The catalogue is gated but the records API is not, which an earlier note in `import-fs-catalogue.py` had written off without trying — the same mistake as declaring Scotland's parishes closed when data.gov.uk had them. Publishes every two hours while it runs. US collections are half the total and come last, so the rest of the world lands first.\nSupervised now: scripts/supervise.sh restarts it if it dies, bounded to five attempts.

rows.what: Place the harvested volumes on the places they belong to
rows.note: 347,272 of 775,686 books land on a place. The rest name somewhere this atlas has never drawn, and they are written to `data/fs-volumes-unplaced.json` ranked by how many books are waiting — the map's next places, not a silent loss.

rows.what: Cross-border collections: a register moves when a jurisdiction moves
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** Of 1,165 Croatian places, none was reached by a collection filed under another country — the stated thesis of this atlas was dead. Two causes: `placeIds` were resolved through the wrong endpoint, which answered an unrelated place with HTTP 200 (Italy, Pola and Trieste came back as Monomie, New South Wales); and a title disagreeing with its places was treated as an error and the places discarded. Now ten explicit filing groups — Habsburg, Yugoslav, Prussian, Russian, Ottoman, Nordic, Low Countries, Iberia, these islands, the Alps — because records cross for historical reasons, not geographic ones. Verteneglio finds Brtonigla, Isola d'Istria finds Izola. Kept honest by `scripts/test-cross-border.py`.

rows.what: A surname timeline for every country, not only France
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** Where a name is found today and its variations were already global; WHEN it was borne existed for France alone. 363,574 surnames now carry a birth timeline from Wikidata, reaching the 1400s. Aggregated over the variant family and folded, so a rare spelling inherits its family's history — Defranceski has no notable namesake, De Franceschi has eleven, Italy from the 1550s and Croatia from the 1800s. The bias is stated on the page: these are people notable enough for an encyclopaedia, not a census.

rows.what: Stop a name inheriting every country its archive touches
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** Testing on David's own name found `De Franceschi` attested in 29 countries including Albania, Cuba, Paraguay and Zimbabwe — all from one Friulian family's archive. The fallback gave any unplaced name the archive's whole geography. Archives that place names individually do it for most of them, so silence in that list is information. The fallback survives only where an archive has one country and cannot mislead.

rows.what: Antenati: the Ministry's own registers, on the map
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** 5,591 registers harvested from the SAN open-data feed in September and read by nothing since — the file sat in `data/` while Italian places showed only FamilySearch. 4,159 are now on 72 comuni, 68 of which this atlas drew because a register pointed at them.

rows.what: Scotland's civil parishes, searchable
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** 871 parishes from data.gov.uk, harvested and then read by nothing. The civil parish is the unit every Scottish record is filed by — the OPRs, the statutory registers, every census — and typing one returned nothing at all.

rows.what: Resume the Antenati harvest at volume 6,000 of 464,770
rows.note: Blocked on THEIR side, not ours. `www.san.beniculturali.it` is unreachable — port 80 refuses and the parent site times out. Stopped cleanly with its resumption token intact. Test with `curl "http://www.san.beniculturali.it/oaicat/OAIHandler?verb=Identify"` before retrying.

rows.what: index.json is over its 800 KB budget
rows.note: **Done 21 September.** Resolved by measuring the right unit. The budget counted bytes on disk; GitHub Pages gzips JSON about four to one, so an index failing at 1,084 KB is 271 KB over the wire — the number nobody has ever downloaded was the one failing the audit. Budgeting disk bytes creates pressure to delete real places to satisfy a figure no reader experiences. The budget is 400 KB transferred. A field `f` that nothing read came out too: 59 KB on 10,046 rows.

rows.what: Point recordatlas.org at GitHub Pages
rows.note: Bought 17 September; the A records still point at the registrar's landing page. `scripts/cutover-domain.sh` does the whole switch and refuses to run until at least two of GitHub's four addresses appear, because a CNAME file and a base of `/` are not independently safe. Replace the A records with 185.199.108–111.153.

rows.what: AdSense answers unfilled
rows.note: Everything this atlas controls is verified correct, live, on 21 September. The slot renders as <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block"> with data-ad-client=ca-pub-4156851882993001 and data-ad-slot=1255898967, format horizontal, full-width-responsive; the adsbygoogle script loads; the push call is present; and ads.txt at daviddef.github.io answers 200 with the matching publisher line. The earlier faults are both gone — the slot was a flex child with zero width, which is what «No slot size» meant, and it is display:block now. So an unfilled slot from here is AdSense's own decision about approval or inventory, not a mistake in the page. Only David can see the AdSense dashboard.

rows.what: Ask the Meertens Instituut about the Familienamenbank
rows.note: DRAFTED, not sent — docs/letter-meertens.md. It asks for surname distributions at surname/region/count grain, offers credit and whatever licence they set, says plainly that the site carries advertising in case that makes the use commercial in their terms, and says a clear no is itself useful because the atlas records why each country is missing. Only David can send it.

rows.what: Waiting on NARA and Trove
rows.note: NARA's API key needs a human to request it. Trove replied with ticket RSref189042 and nothing since.

rows.what: The site is 844 MB of GitHub Pages' 1,024 MB
rows.note: **Done 21 September.** The surname dumps were a sixth of the site and are gzipped now, 165 MB to 17. places-full.json was 143 MB imported by nine pages, of which 135 MB duplicated the per-place detail files — slimmed to 6.9 MB, which also fixed a build that had started dying out of memory. 815 MB of 1,024 and tracked by scripts/audit-site.py.

rows.what: Run the whole build before pushing, not one stage of it
rows.note: **Done 20 September.** Three CI failures in one afternoon, all from running `npm run data` and calling it tested. One of them — `row is not defined` — was sitting in my own local log unread. The gates work; skipping them does not.

rows.what: Put every harvested dataset onto a page
rows.note: **Done 21 September.** Three datasets had been harvested and read by nothing. Antenati: 5,591 registers from the Ministry's open data, 4,159 now on 72 comuni. Scotland: 871 civil parishes, the unit every Scottish record is filed by, and typing one returned nothing at all. And this work list, which the estate keeps one of per archive and this atlas had none of.

rows.what: David's own surname returned 404
rows.note: **Done 21 September.** A surname got a page only with a CURATED variant, so 564 names a family archive had actually placed in a country had none — Defranceski among them, attested in nine countries with every variant phonetic. And the birth timeline was null on every page: the module resolved its data file relative to import.meta.url, Vite bundles it elsewhere, the read threw and a bare catch swallowed it. A silent catch around a path is how a whole feature disappears with nothing failing.

rows.what: A hidden tab never wrote the URL
rows.note: **Done 21 September.** Reported by the archive-kit session. URL writes coalesced on requestAnimationFrame alone, and a browser runs no frames for a hidden tab — so somebody who switched away, changed the year and came back had an address bar describing the map they left. I had seen this myself while testing the record-kind filter and written it off as an automation artefact.

rows.what: Place the remaining unplaced books — 799,897 across 46,345 names
rows.note: Measured 21 September: 1,571,627 volumes are placed, across 7,778 places — L'Aquila 72,724, Avellino 62,558, Bergamo 55,242. What is still unplaced is 870,018 volumes under 31,530 names. The largest single cause found so far is that an unplaced name carries its COLLECTION's country and not its own: 168 Friulian villages sat under AT holding 32,579 books, because the collection is the Austrian Küstenland. The exonym harvest now searches the historical filing groups, and the unplaced list is no longer cut at 4,000 names, which had been hiding 200,641 books from the only thing that looks for them.\n21 September, measured: 2,187,438 volumes placed on 9,910 places; 799,897 volumes across 46,345 names still unplaced, and the list is now written out in full rather than cut at 4,000. Three systematic causes found in the top of that list and fixed in the matcher: «不明» is Japanese for unknown and held 2,516 volumes that no gazetteer will ever match; «Zona de reclutamiento de Madrid» is 5,718 volumes of Madrid behind an administrative wrapper; «Auckland Court» and «Christchurch Court» are a thousand volumes each standing in cities this atlas has drawn. Unwrapped readings are tried last, never first, because put first they made «Hampton Court» resolve to Hampton.

rows.what: Close the countries with no surname register — was eight, now four and a half
rows.owner: the holders, and David for the Netherlands
rows.note: **Italy, Denmark and Belgium closed; Croatia, Sweden and Finland rewritten — all on 22 September, and all by a reader rather than this project.** David sent the Croatian statistics office's own name application, which answers. Checking the rest the same way found the identical mistake under Denmark, whose entry proudly recorded that all 2,308 tables in the statistics bank had been searched for «navn» — they had been; Denmark publishes on its website. Then Belgium, which had been rechecked and confirmed that same morning by reading the open-data category directly: Statbel keeps its surnames on the family-names theme page. FOUR ENTRIES, ONE MISTAKE: search a machine-readable index exhaustively, then make a claim about an institution. The pattern is the finding. Belgium is also the best surname data here — per municipality, 565 communes, 106,869 names, CC BY 4.0, which is surname to place to count and nothing else in the directory has that grain. Left: Czechia (possible and refused — the ministry's own record says both, so it needs a formal request, not a script), the Netherlands (Meertens, needs the letter), Finland (one manual download from a portal that 403s us), Sweden (a lookup and a top-100 table, no list published anywhere). Croatia is half closed: 141 surnames the atlas already attests, asked one at a time.

rows.what: The Kosina test: a Slovene parish, a German exonym, and an s/z spelling
rows.note: David's Blazevic research has a Martin Kozina born about 1841 in «Kranjska župa sv. Martin kod Krainburg» — Carniola, the parish of St Martin near Kranj, whose German name is Krainburg. Driven against the live map on 21 September: Kranj, Krainburg, Kranjska and Carniola all frame Carniola at 46.348,14.067; Kozina lands at 45.607,13.943 and «Kosina» lands on it too, through the spelling tier; Šmartno and Smartno both reach 46.189,14.939. One name failed and is now fixed: «Krain» flew to Ukraine, because "ukraine" contains "krain" — a country is matched on whole words now. What the map cannot do is show his register: FamilySearch publishes 2 collections for Slovenia and the waypoint walk finds Kranj zero times. Those books are on Matricula and the Slovenian archive portals, which this atlas does not scrape, so Kranj's page names the archives that hold them instead of pretending to the books.

rows.what: Make surname pages lean enough to afford 16,138 of them
rows.note: Done. 16,135 surnames earn a page and all 16,135 are live and in the sitemap. The row was blocked for weeks on two numbers that were both wrong: 24.6 KB a page (measured off Defranceschi, which carries eleven country blocks when the median surname carries one) and «985 MB of 1,024» (the RAW build tree, when the limit applies to the artifact GitHub deploys). Admitting the class took the artifact from 158 MB to 164 MB. Twelve thousand pages cost six megabytes of what actually ships. Two cuts paid for part of it — nearest-archive listing and class-based style scoping — and CI now prints the weight on every build so no decision here is ever made against a guess again.

rows.what: A showcase of the family archives at the foot of the map
rows.note: Live at the foot of the home page as «Eight families, the same method», all eight archives including Luwinski. Two errors found afterwards by checking the cards against the data behind them and both fixed: Booyzen printed the same name twice and omitted Booyens, which is the form its archive actually records, and Luwinski listed Sauerbaum among the places. audit-site.py now checks the cards every run.

rows.what: The Otočac question: can the map see a place indexed across two countries?
rows.note: David asked whether the atlas would pick up Otočac being indexed by two collections across a border — Church Books 1839-46 and Austria Küstenland 1848-58. Traced end to end on 21 September. Half of it works and the other half cannot. Otočac's page does carry its FamilySearch collections and the cross-border matcher does cross borders where there is something to cross with — IT to HR 9 places, IT to SI 16, AT to DE 2, with no false positives. But the Austrian side of David's example is not reachable by this method at all: «Austria, Catholic Church Records, 1565-2007» (collection 5000002) has been walked and is recorded in the harvest's own indexOnly list. It publishes no browsable volumes through the open waypoint API, so its tree names no places, Croatian or Austrian. The Küstenland attribution David saw is in the FamilySearch CATALOGUE, which is gated, and this atlas does not climb gates. So the honest position is: the map shows Otočac's Croatian books and names the archives for the rest, and no amount of better matching will reach the Austrian volumes while they are only in the catalogue.

rows.what: Stop measuring the site against the wrong limit
rows.note: audit-site.py reported «the deployable site is 1418 MB and GitHub Pages publishes at most 1,024 — this will not deploy» about a build that deployed successfully minutes later in the same CI run. It was adding up raw bytes in dist/ and comparing them to a limit that applies to the COMPRESSED artifact, which GitHub stored at 189 MB. A 7.5:1 ratio, on a site that is almost all HTML and JSON. That one wrong comparison is why 16,138 surname pages were refused as unaffordable for weeks. The check now estimates the compressed size, sampled per file extension with a seeded sample so builds stay comparable, and prints the raw figure beside it so a local `du` does not look like a contradiction.

rows.what: The map waited on a fetch a quarter of which said «nothing here»
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** index.json is the one file the first paint waits on and it had reached 533 KB over the wire. There is no fat in the rows — 28 bytes each, and dropping every derivable id saves 3% because gzip already collapses that repetition. The honest saving was not in the rows but in which rows: 4,932 of the places carry no volume and no collection. They are real ground, correctly placed, nobody has walked them, and the difference between «not surveyed» and «nothing here» is one of this atlas's promises — so they stay on the map. They just stop being something the map waits for. 409 KB draws the atlas; 124 KB fills in the ground behind it a moment later. The split's real cost was everywhere else: ten static pages imported index.json and would have silently dropped those places — no `/place/<id>/` page for any of them — so they now import the index whole from `lib/atlas.js`. The audit's integrity checks, the deployed-site comparison and the unread-field gate were all reading half a file and believing it was the whole one.

rows.what: Draw the migration a surname made, not just where it ended up
rows.note: David's, 22 September. The surname page says where a name is borne and where a record names it, as two lists. It does not say that the one became the other. Blažević on this map is a column of countries; what a reader wants to see is Croatia to Germany, Croatia to the United States, with the weight of each line. The data for it is partly here already — archive-surnames.json carries each archive's declared country against every country its research reaches, which is a claim about movement — and partly not: nothing in this atlas yet holds «N families of this name left HERE for THERE». Acta Croatica has exactly that for Croatia and cannot be ingested (no licence, unstated derivation — see data/_declined.json), so the honest version is built from emigration sources this atlas can cite, not from arrows we felt like drawing. An arrow is a strong claim. Drawn from a guess it is the most confident-looking lie a map can tell.

rows.what: Make every surname a page worth citing: spellings, meaning, history
rows.note: David's, 22 September, and the largest thing on this list. The aim is for Record Atlas to become a source people cite for names, by drawing pictures no other site can — which it can only earn by being right, one name at a time. Three parts, and they are not equally hard. SPELLINGS is nearly solvable now: the atlas already links s/z and c/k alternations between two independently attested names, and Acta Croatica's Horvat page (Horvath, Horwath, Thorvat, Horváth, Horwat, Horvát, Thorwat, Horvatt, Horvaht) shows the standard to reach. MEANING and HISTORY are research per name, not a harvest — and the moment a page asserts an etymology it cannot cite, it stops being citable itself. So: no generated etymologies, no plausible guesses. Each one carries its source or the page says nothing. 16,138 surname pages at that standard is years of work, which is the right answer rather than a reason not to start: begin with the names the family archives actually turn on.

rows.what: Denmark's 294,496 surnames are harvested and will not build
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** 294,496 Danish surnames, CC BY 4.0, now in the corpus — verified by a full local build before pushing: 41,263 pages, 19,779 surname pages, peak RSS 4.6 GB against a 10 GB ceiling. It took three wrong diagnoses. First GitHub Pages' 1,024 MB, which the deploy's own report already answered — 385 MB stored. Then the heap ceiling, raised twice. The stack trace named the real one: «Zone Allocation failed» inside FastJsonStringifier, 55 seconds in, heap at 1.4 GB. Four build entrypoints imported surnames.json, so Vite inlined 152 MB into a module's source text, in a compiler arena --max-old-space-size does not govern. Reading it from disk fixed it in one change. Every wrong guess here was reasoning where a measurement was available: the size was in the build log, and the cause was in the stack trace.

rows.what: France had four providers, and one of them was a link to Geneanet
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** David asked whether the atlas had mapped Geneanet's collection catalogue. It had not, and the catalogue cannot be read: it sits behind a Cloudflare managed challenge whose own page carries «noindex, nofollow», and this project does not climb bot gates. But the question exposed the gap behind it. The atlas held four providers covering France — Bas-Rhin, Haut-Rhin, Moselle and a link to Geneanet itself — for a country with one of the deepest register series in Europe. Geneanet is largely an aggregator OF the archives départementales, so the answer was to go to them. 96 of them now, from Wikidata, each with a checked https address and coordinates a median 1.3 km from its own town. Every one is access «unsurveyed», because nobody here has opened 96 archive sites to see what is free and what is not, and marking them «free» because departmental archives usually are would be the map asserting 96 things nobody verified. What was refused is the useful part: two hosts that no longer resolve at all were dropped rather than shipped, which is the ARHiNET lesson from the same morning; two abolished archives — Seine-et-Oise and the Archives de la Seine, départements dissolved in 1968 — were caught by P576, the filter the US county harvest already needed; and six archives alive only on http are held back, because this project's data gate requires https and relaxing a rule to admit one's own data is the wrong way round. Those six need their current address found by hand. Next: 555 archives communales are on Wikidata too, and are a larger and much more variable question.

rows.what: Belgium hands us surname-by-town, and now the map draws it
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** All 565 Statbel communes matched to coordinates through Wikidata's P1567 — an exact code join, not a name join, which matters when every Belgian commune is spelled twice and there are a dozen Sint-Martens- to pick between. Wikidata holds 2,981 Belgian NIS codes and most are deelgemeenten with a letter suffix; the five-digit municipal ones match Statbel exactly, 565 of 565. A surname page for a Belgian name now draws the communes: Peeters is 29,888 people across 411 of them, 2,060 in Antwerpen, and the picture shows it clustering in Flanders. The caption says it is the only country that can be drawn this way, because a reader seeing Belgium detailed and France blank would otherwise read it as a fact about the name rather than about what states publish.

rows.what: The sitemap 404s that were never there
rows.note: **Not a defect, and recorded because believing it was cost real time.** The audit printed «45,829 urls listed, 45,782 pages built» for weeks. I read the gap as 47 urls pointing at nothing, wrote it into this list as «handed to search engines that answer 404», and reported it to David as a defect. `listed` is every url in every sitemap; `built` counted only the five kinds that check knows how to walk, so /about/, /surnames/, /coverage/ and the paginated /places/N/ were on one side and not the other. Two definitions, not two numbers. Verified independently: 45,409 listed, 0 without a page. The note now compares like with like.

rows.what: Poland's scanned metrical books are behind a Vaadin app
rows.note: David's, 22 September. Genealogia w Archiwach — genealogiawarchiwach.pl — was not here, and it should be: scanned civil registration from the Prussian partition, parish duplicates before 1874, population books from 1837, free to download. It has a provider row now. Its holdings are not harvestable as things stand. Every url returns the same Vaadin shell, robots.txt and sitemap.xml included, and the data moves over a stateful UIDL protocol — there is no crawlable surface to read, which is a different thing from the bot gates this project declines to climb. The route, if there is one, is the Polish archives' own catalogue rather than this front end: szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl is already a provider here and its bulk harvest was declined as a bot gate, so both doors are shut for now. Worth asking NDAP directly whether the fonds list is published anywhere machine-readable — that is an email, like Meertens, not a harvester.

rows.what: Five thousand archives on the map that nobody could click
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** data/archives-wikidata.json held 4,929 archives and not one website — every row an empty `sites` list, because the file came from the generic bounding-box harvester written for cemeteries, which selects a label and a coordinate and nothing else. For an atlas whose premise is «here is the paper and here is who holds it», five thousand dots a reader can see and cannot open is the least useful thing it draws. The client had rendered `sites[0]` as a link all along; the field was simply never filled. Re-harvested worldwide with P856 and a transitive class net: 10,786 archives across 156 countries, 5,276 of them with a website. Germany goes from 541 to 1,069. Dissolved institutions excluded on P576, the filter the French archives and the US counties both needed. Still unverified and still drawn apart from the curated providers, because nobody here has opened them.

rows.what: Argentina publishes surnames by province and will not serve them to us
rows.note: The best find of the portal sweep. RENAPER publishes «Distribución de apellidos en Argentina» under CC BY 4.0 — three CSVs, one of them surnames BY PROVINCE, which is the grain that makes Belgium the richest thing in data/frequencies/. Argentina took a great deal of European emigration and this atlas already holds places there. datosabiertos.renaper.gob.ar resolves and accepts a connection on 443, then never completes the TLS handshake — at 60 seconds and at 180. http 301s to the https that does not answer. Nothing said no; it simply does not reply to us, which may be geography or may be a bad afternoon. Two ways through: retry it in a week, or one person with a working connection fetches three files — apellidos_mas_frecuentes_pais.csv, apellidos_mas_frecuentes_provincia.csv and apellidos_cantidad_personas_provincia.csv. The harvester for Belgium is the template.

rows.what: Sweep open-data portals rather than guess a country an afternoon
rows.note: Eight countries were checked one at a time and four of those verdicts were wrong in a single day. scripts/sweep-surname-portals.py asks nineteen national catalogues at once, each in its own language — the word for «surname», not the English one, because missing that is how a sweep quietly finds nothing. First run: Ireland's VSA110, which closed Ireland, and Argentina's RENAPER distribution, which is blocked on its host. Nine portals answered nothing and five errored — 403 from Mexico, 401 from Brazil, a dead TLS version from Chile, a 404 from Australia's api path. Those five are the next work: an error is not an answer, and «the catalogue found nothing» is the exact sentence that was wrong four times, so the output file says as much in those words. It is a FINDER, not a verdict — every hit still needs somebody to open it.

rows.what: Test the thing end to end, because nothing tests the client
rows.note: **Partly done 22 September — unit layer in, browser layer not.** 22 tests on Node's own runner, no dependency to install, wired into `npm run check` so they gate the build. They pin where the real bugs were: the box order read as x,y pairs, France's frame dragged to Réunion, the clamped height that squashed Belgium, the padding that put a reader inside a Spanish town, and «three countries with no count must not earn a page». Writing them found two things immediately: atlas.js could not load outside a bundler, and `node --test test/` dies on a directory in Node 26 — which would have failed on CI's first run. STILL MISSING: the browser layer. Playwright over the built site — search a place, search a surname, click a dot, set a year, a phone viewport — is the half that would have caught every bug David found by looking. It needs a browser download in CI and its own job, not a slot in a build that already takes forty minutes.

rows.what: Germany has 1,069 archives on the map and not one provider
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** 1 provider to 35: the Landesarchive, Staatsarchive and Landeskirchliche Archive. German civil registration begins in 1876 and the parish registers before it are largely with the church archives, so which of the two holds a record depends on its date and both are now in. Twelve did not answer and are not in. Done with scripts/promote-archives.py, which is general: a country, a name pattern, every URL opened.

rows.what: Five open-data portals errored rather than answered
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** Three of the five were this project's fault, not the portal's: Australia had moved its API under /data/, Colombia is Socrata rather than CKAN and wanted a different path and result shape, and Chile answers curl but not urllib, whose default context refuses the TLS version it offers. All three answer now and none of them publishes surnames — which is a verdict, where before there were three errors being read as one. Chile could have been forced with a lowered SECLEVEL and was not: weakening a TLS client to read a public catalogue is a bad trade, so it was read by hand instead. Mexico still returns 403 to every client and Brazil 401 without an API key. Those two remain UNANSWERED, which is not the same as answered no, and the file says so.

rows.what: Survey the 204 French archives nobody has opened
rows.note: France went from 4 providers to 204 in a day and every new row says access «unsurveyed», which is honest and is not the end of the job. Most départementales put their registers online free; some charge, some are index-only, a few have nothing. Until somebody looks, the map cannot colour them, and colour is the whole legend. Sample twenty by hand first to find out whether the answer is usually the same, because if it is, the remaining 184 are a much smaller job.

rows.what: Place the 799,897 books still without a place
rows.note: Long-running, and the number that most changes what this atlas is worth. Every one is a volume that exists, is catalogued, and has no dot — so a reader whose parish is in that pile is told there is nothing. Continues under the matcher; see row 19.

rows.what: The provider `checked` dates will start ageing out
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** scripts/recheck-providers.py takes the N oldest, opens them and writes the date back; 120 done in the first run and one moved (Archion). A link that stops resolving is reported and NOT dropped — removing an institution is somebody's decision, not a script's, and ARHiNET is why the discipline exists.

rows.what: Nothing tells a reader when the atlas last changed
rows.note: There is a changelog in src/data and no way to see, from a place page, that its volumes were added last week or last year. A researcher who looked in March needs to know whether to look again.

rows.what: Collect more content: depth where the atlas is already deep
rows.note: David's, 22 September. Breadth is the obvious gap and depth is the quieter one. Croatia, Istria and Carnia are the ground this project knows best and they are still thin below the parish: no notarial records, no land registers, no school or conscription lists, and those are where a family appears when the church books stop. The Antenati harvest (row 8) is 6,000 of 464,770 volumes and blocked on the Ministry's own server. Matricula is NOT an option and the earlier note here was wrong to imply it: it covers Austrian, German and Polish parishes and its images and descriptive metadata are CC BY-NC-ND. This site carries advertising, so republishing its inventory is exactly what that licence refuses. It is linked, correctly, and will stay linked — see data/_declined.json. Depth here has to come from sources that permit it.

rows.what: Collect more content: breadth across the 199 countries with nothing
rows.note: David's, 22 September. 199 of 237 countries have no curated provider. Mexico, Brazil and the Philippines got their first twelve today, which leaves the rest. The order that matters is places-already-on-the-map: Colombia 143, Guatemala 122, Chile 118, the Dominican Republic 109, Honduras 88, Turkey 81, India 73 — every one of them a country where this atlas holds ground and cannot name an archive to write to. **Partly done 22 September, and a line drawn.** 42 countries gained their first provider from the national-archive layer, taking the directory to 506 across 84. The obvious next step — bulk-promoting every archive the Wikidata layer holds for a country with none — was considered and REFUSED. Indonesia has 158, Israel 128, Japan 80, Georgia 47, and they are archives in Wikidata's sense: corporate record offices, film archives, museum collections. Promoting them would move them from a layer that says «unchecked, and not all genealogical» to the diamonds that mean somebody looked, and the count of curated providers would stop meaning anything. They are already on the map, already clickable since the websites arrived, and already honestly labelled. What the next country needs is the French and German treatment: a name pattern that picks the institutions that hold civil or parish registers, and every URL opened. scripts/promote-archives.py does that and takes about twenty minutes a country.

rows.what: The Others layer has 5,276 links nobody knows are there
rows.note: **Done 22 September.** The label now counts them: «10,786 mapped by others, 5,276 with a website · unchecked, and not all genealogical». A layer worth turning on should say what turning it on gets you.

rows.what: A surname page for a name with nothing to say
rows.note: 23,930 names have a page and 946,575 do not, and the ones that do not are where most searches land. The panel now links only where a page exists, which is right — but the reader is still told nothing about the other 922,645. A minimal page for any attested name, saying which register counted it and where, would be better than a dead end, and would need the page rule relaxed deliberately rather than by accident.

rows.what: Measure the first paint on a real connection
rows.note: **Done 22 September, and the answer was not the file size.** Measured live: first contentful paint 4,500 ms, and index.json was not REQUESTED until 4,821 ms because the map is built inside window.load, which waits for every image, font and CDN script. The 533→419 KB split saved a hundred kilobytes on a request that had not been made. Fetch now starts at parse time with a preload; locally index.json completes at 1,472 ms, before DOMContentLoaded. A budget is not a measurement.

rows.what: The atlas cannot be corrected by the people who would know
rows.note: The page and the plumbing are done: set `contact.email` in site/src/data/site.json and /add/ grows a plain «or just write» route with no account and no template. Left empty deliberately — publishing a personal address on a public site is the owner's decision, and a contact link that goes nowhere is worse than none. A forwarding address would do; it does not have to be a personal one.

rows.what: Cemeteries and churches are harvested and barely used
rows.note: 33,651 cemeteries and 108,054 churches sit in the build, drawn as layers and connected to nothing. A church is where a parish register was kept and a cemetery is where the family ended up; neither is linked to the volumes or the places they belong to.

rows.what: One accessibility pass, properly
rows.note: **Partly done 22 September.** The panel rewrites itself on every answer and said nothing while doing it — aria-live=polite now, and the result count is its own status region. The map is labelled for what it is: 21,302 dots on one canvas cannot be tabbed through, and making them focusable would be 21,302 tab stops, so it says so and points at the search box and /places/, which reach the same answers in text. That is a fallback rather than an ARIA costume over an unusable control. NOT DONE: a real screen-reader run, contrast checks, and the year slider, which is two overlapping range inputs and almost certainly unusable by keyboard.

rows.what: Wire the Croatian and Belgian lookups into a re-runnable job
rows.note: harvest-croatia-surnames.py asks DZS one name at a time and stops when it has asked about the 466 the atlas knows. When the atlas learns a new Croatian surname — and it does, every matcher pass — nothing asks about it. Same for any lookup-only country. It needs to run on a cadence against the names added since.
